newsitem.title: RWANDA: FEATURE-For Rwanda's inmates, living conditions are grim.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-For Rwanda's inmates, living conditions are grim.

text.p: A four-by-two-foot area of wooden boards on the second level of a three-tier bunk in a communal cell of 160 prisoners is Laurent Nzibikamanzi's home.

"This is where I live, where I eat, sleep and have my possessions," said Nzibikamanzi, one of 1,993 inmates in Kibungo prison, built in the 1930s and located 120 km (75 miles) southeast of the capital Kigali.

"There is no privacy. You lie at night asleep with people next to your face, two feet below you, and two feet above you. For a year I have never been more than two feet from another person," Nzibikamanzi told Reuters at the prison.

Around him in the semi-darkness -- filled with the pungent stench of sweat, excrement, dirty clothing and stale food -- are perched hundreds of men, jostling for inches of space as they eat a midday meal of manioc and beans.
Blankets, tins, clothing, shoes, scraps of hoarded cardboard and plastic sheeting are suspended from the ceiling by string.
Conditions are increasingly grim for the 90,000 mostly Hutu inmates held like Nzibikamanzi in Rwanda's 10 major prisons on suspected participation in the country's 1994 genocide.

The first trials for such suspects were launched late last month in Rwanda. Death penalties have already been handed down to a few of those convicted for the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 mainly minority ethnic Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
SPREAD OF DISEASE A CONCERN
The floors of the cells in Kibungo prison are always wet, soaked down with chlorinated disinfectant to prevent the spread of disease.
"The problems here are dysentery, malaria and TB," said prison governor Manasse Sebagabo.

Outside the lines of dark, unlit lavatory cabinets, soaked with chlorinated water, dozens of men with chronic diarrhoea queue for a place. In one, three men share the same hole. Bottles of dirty water replace toilet paper.
Sickness is not the only worry.

In the juvenile cell, home to 73 boys under 18, lines of adolescent males swing their feet from the edge of bunks, hold hands, sleep and play draughts in their quarters, even more cramped than the other prisoners.
There is no door, and no attempt has been made to separate them from the older prisoners.

A prisoner who gave his name only as Anastase said: "Rights to have sex with the boys is one thing we barter. Some tobacco or food will get you half an hour with one of them. Other prisoners keep your privacy while you are with them."
The governor said tobacco, alcohol and drugs were not allowed in the prison "but on the weekly visits there is always a way to get (them) in."

Other prisoners said food, tobacco and sex was traded for rights to a place to sit in the shade of the prison yard, where prisoners sit jammed three to a square metre of dirty, sodden concrete. Above the open yard is the bright blue of the sky.
SOME PRISONERS RETURNED FROM TANZANIA

Discipline in the prison is assured by "captains," or warders picked from inmates. Outside the prison orange-uniformed guards toting Kalshnikovs search 119 new arrivals brought in from a communal detention centre in nearby Zaza parish.
"Among these people are many Hutus who have recently returned from Tanzanian refugee camps," said an employee of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR.
"At least things will be better here for them."
Just inside the prison gate are the tiny isolation cells holding Egide Gatanaze and Deogratias Bizimana, two of the first people to receive the death penalty in the genocide trials.
Said Deputy Justice Minister Gerard Gahima: "At least now the trials have started we can release some of the pressure on the prisons."
